analysis.one_liner: Requires FDA oversight of lab-developed medical tests, with public disclosure of their accuracy.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: it sat in the Senate Health Committee until the 2007-2009 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bring laboratory-developed tests — medical tests designed and run inside a lab, including genetic tests sold directly to consumers — under Food and Drug Administration oversight for the first time. Labs would have to register, label each test with its intended use and whether it was FDA-cleared, and submit evidence of the test's accuracy to a public, searchable database. Tests sold directly to consumers would require a doctor's order, and tests that flunked review would be pulled off the market. The bill was introduced by Sen. Edward Kennedy in March 2007 with one Republican cosponsor and never received any committee or floor action.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take medical or genetic tests. Today many such tests are designed and marketed by labs with no FDA review; this bill would require honest labeling of intended use and clearance status, a public database of evidence on each test's accuracy, and a doctor's order before direct-to-consumer genetic tests. Doctors ordering tests would also get better information.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients taking medical and genetic tests

how_it_helps.text: Declares every laboratory-developed test to be a medical device, bringing it under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act's labeling, registration, and adverse-event reporting rules [S2] [S3].

Requires labs to submit evidence of a test's analytical and clinical validity to a public, searchable FDA database, so doctors and patients can see whether a test actually works for its advertised purpose [S2] [S3].

Reclassifies direct-to-consumer tests as prescription tests that require a licensed practitioner's authorization, and requires a 510(k) report for direct-to-consumer tests within 180 days of enactment [S3].
Lets the FDA pull a test from the market when a lab fails to submit required evidence or the test is not cleared or approved for its intended use [S3].

Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to issue a rule setting proficiency-testing standards for labs that run genetic tests, and to provide enhanced federal reimbursement for tests that have been cleared or approved [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medical laboratories that develop their own tests, including hospital labs and the then-emerging direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies. They would bear registration, evidence-submission, and FDA review costs, some tests would be restricted or pulled from the market, and federal programs would be steered toward reimbursing FDA-cleared tests.
analysis.who_pays_short: Clinical labs and genetic testing companies

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs could raise the price of tests or reduce their availability, particularly for small or hospital labs whose specialized tests have never gone through FDA review [S3].
Requiring a prescription for direct-to-consumer tests limits the ability of people to get their own genetic information without going through a doctor [S3].
Enhanced federal reimbursement only for cleared or approved tests could steer coverage toward established products and away from newer lab-developed tests, even ones that work [S3].

The bill gives labs a partial inspection exemption for class II tests and lets CLIA lab standards satisfy some FDA manufacturing requirements unless the Secretary finds otherwise, an accommodation that lightens the regulatory load on the industry [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real gap: at the time, FDA did not review laboratory-developed tests, so a test could be sold to consumers without any demonstrated accuracy or disclosure of its clearance status. The transparency gains for patients are substantial. The costs fall on labs, and the prescription requirement and reimbursement tilt would have trade-offs for access and innovation. The bill included industry accommodations — softer inspection rules, a two-year delay before FDA could move most prescription tests to the highest-risk class, and letting existing CLIA lab standards satisfy some FDA requirements — which would have softened the compliance burden, though critics could fairly call those carve-outs too generous.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read it twice and sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never considered it, and the bill died there when the 2007-2009 Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the Laboratory Test Improvement Act on March 1, 2007, joined by one Republican cosponsor [S1] [S4] [S5].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No committee markup, vote, or further action is recorded; the bill never left committee before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Laboratory-developed test providers and direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies avoided the new registration, evidence, and FDA review requirements. Patients gained nothing from the bill's death: tests remained outside FDA oversight, with no public database of evidence on accuracy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Test labs avoided FDA oversight; patients got nothing

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — one Democrat and one Republican — but no party ever had to vote on it because it never left committee.

industries.note: Labs that design their own tests would have to register with the FDA, label intended use and clearance status, submit accuracy evidence to a public database, and stop selling tests that flunk review. Their interest in avoiding evidence requirements runs against patients' interest in knowing whether a test works.

The bill would reclassify consumer genetic tests as prescription tests and require an FDA 510(k) submission within six months, cutting companies off from selling directly to consumers. Selling unvalidated tests to consumers without a doctor conflicts with patient safety.

Regulation of competing lab-developed tests would level a playing field where cleared products previously faced unregulated rivals, and federal health programs would provide enhanced reimbursement for cleared and approved tests. Better-validated tests benefit patients too.
